title: Add interceptors with proxies
goal: By the end you can add @Timed and @Retry to the container's components, through a JDK proxy for components with interfaces and a Byte Buddy subclass for the rest, with correct equals and hashCode, default methods retried call by call, and a start-up error instead of a silent skip when Kotlin's final classes get in the way.
opening:
The city's booking service runs in another building, and the box office reaches it over the network. Most calls come back in a few milliseconds. Now and then one gets no answer: the call times out, and the customer at the counter waits for nothing. So the theatre wants every booking call timed, and a call that timed out tried again.

Writing a timer and a retry loop into every method works, and buries each line of real work under a dozen lines of plumbing. The stand-in at the stage door from the Class loading track did this job for an actor: it noted every request and tried again when the actor didn't answer. The trap is in what you try again. Retry the wrong call, and one customer ends up holding two seats.

Last time, the container built each part from its constructor. In this lesson, it hands out stand-ins, objects called proxies that take each call first: a JDK proxy for a part with an interface, a Byte Buddy subclass for one without. Then we'll make Kotlin's final classes fail loudly and choose which call to retry. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `close(night)` is annotated `@Retry(attempts = 3)` and calls `this.verify(night)`, which is also `@Retry(attempts = 3)` and always throws a failure that is worth retrying. The part is intercepted by a subclass proxy, so self-calls are intercepted. How many times does `verify`'s body run before `close` gives up?
warmup.why: Each attempt of `close` calls `verify` through the subclass, and `verify`'s own retry runs its body three times before it throws. `close`'s retry then catches that and tries again, three times in all: 3 x 3 = 9. Nested retries multiply. With a forwarding proxy the inner call would skip interception and run once per `close` attempt, 3 in all, which is why 3 is the tempting answer.

sections.h: A part with an interface gets a stand-in at the stage door: a JDK proxy
sections.body:
For each component, the container now decides how its interceptors will run. If the component implements an interface, it gets a JDK proxy. `Proxy.newProxyInstance` writes a class that implements the interfaces and sends every call to one `InvocationHandler`, as Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy showed: the stand-in at the stage door, with the actor behind it. The container creates the real object first, the **target**, and the proxy holds it. Spring Framework documents the same rule for its own proxies: if the target implements at least one interface, it uses a JDK proxy. (Spring Boot, its quick-start layer, switches the default to subclasses, as Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors showed.)

That lesson's rules for the handler come back as the four cases you write in the lab, in this order:

1. `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` arrive with `method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class`. Answer them on the proxy itself, by identity. A handler that sends `equals` to the target makes `proxy.equals(proxy)` false, and `list.remove(proxy)` quietly fails.
2. A default method, an interface method with a body, goes to `InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args)`. Its body then runs with `this` being the proxy, so the calls inside it come back through the handler.
3. Every other method gets an `Invocation` with that method's chain, ending in `method.invoke(target, args)`.
4. That last call catches `InvocationTargetException` and throws its cause, so the caller sees the booking service's own `BookingUnavailableException`, not a wrapper around it.

The demo puts the container's proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, `equals` included:

```text
bean class: jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5 implements [BookingClient]
container's handler  p.equals(p)=true  listeners.remove(p)=true  hashCode is identity=true
forward everything   p.equals(p)=false  listeners.remove(p)=false  hashCode is identity=false
```

The forwarding stand-in asked the actor whether the actor was the stand-in, and the actor said no. Fair enough.

Two consequences follow from "the proxy implements the interfaces", and both surprise people. First, the object you get back isn't a `FlakyBooking`. It's a `$Proxy5` that implements `BookingClient`. `get(BookingClient.class)` works, but `get(FlakyBooking.class)` can't return it, so the lab's container refuses with a message that names the interface to ask for:

```text
FlakyBooking is behind a JDK proxy that implements [BookingClient]; ask for one of those, not for the class
```

Second, the handler only ever sees the interface's `Method`, so the annotations must sit on the interface. `@Timed` on the class's method would never be read, and nothing would say so. The container refuses that case when it starts, rather than skip the timer in silence.

Kotlin's final classes don't matter on this path. `FakeBooking` in the tests is a plain, final Kotlin class, and that's fine: the JDK needs only the interface. A part without an interface is a different story.

sections.h: A part without an interface gets a costume copy: a Byte Buddy subclass, so final is fatal
sections.body:
`ShowCloser` closes the box office after the last show of the night. It checks the night's code, files the night in the archive, and returns a short note. It has no interface, so there is no job card for a stand-in to copy. Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors had the answer: the costume department sews a full copy of the costume, a subclass that extends the class and replaces some of its methods. Byte Buddy, a library that writes classes while your program runs, does the sewing.

Byte Buddy's `subclass(type)` copies the class's public constructors. The container calls the generated `ShowCloser$ByteBuddy$...` constructor with the `ShowArchive` it resolved, and the original class is never created on its own. There is one object. Each intercepted method becomes an override whose `@SuperCall` callable, a small object that runs `super.close(...)`, sits at the end of the chain. A retry simply calls it again.

Because the subclass is the object, a self-call, a call from one of the object's methods to another through `this`, goes through it too. `close` calls `this.verify(night)`. `this` is the subclass, so `verify`'s override runs its own chain. The Class loading track called this the understudy who plays the role, as against the lookalike at the door who passes requests to the actor. The figure shows both: the JDK proxy is the lookalike, and the actor's own calls never pass the door. The lab's test closes night N-17 and reads the log: `[ShowCloser.verify, ShowCloser.close]`. `verify` comes first because each timer records when its call ends, and `verify` ends inside `close`.

A subclass can only intercept what it's allowed to override, and Kotlin makes that a daily problem. A Kotlin class is final unless you write `open`, and so is each of its members: a role nobody may copy. On a final class, Byte Buddy fails loudly: `Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types`. On an `open class` with a plain `fun`, it succeeds and simply leaves the method alone. `@Timed` sits on it and does nothing. That silent case is why the lab's container calls `check(component)` for every component when it starts. It refuses a final class, or a final or private intercepted method, with a message that says what to change. The demo tries two Kotlin classes with the same `@Timed` method, and the build opens only the second:

```text
KFinalPrices: class final=true, feeCents final=true
  refused: KFinalPrices is final, so no subclass can intercept it: make it open, or give it an interface
KOpenedPrices: class final=false, feeCents final=false
  wired as KOpenedPrices$ByteBuddy$w7Szn3cT, timed calls [KOpenedPrices.feeCents]
```

There are three fixes. Write `open` on the class and on each intercepted method. Or let the all-open compiler plugin do it for classes that carry an annotation you choose; this lab's build opens classes marked `@OpenForProxies`:

```kotlin solo
// container/build.gradle.kts
plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") }
allOpen { annotation("workbench.container.l02.demo.OpenForProxies") }
```

`kotlin-spring` is the same plugin, preset to open the classes Spring creates. The third fix is an interface, which moves the part to the JDK proxy path, where finality doesn't matter. (Quarkus goes a fourth way: by default it rewrites final classes while the program is built, so that it can subclass them.)

**An annotation only works if a proxy can reach the method. Make the container refuse what no proxy can reach.**

Each class Byte Buddy writes also gets a class loader of its own, a `ByteArrayClassLoader`, unless you choose another loading strategy. Lesson 3 counts what that leaves behind.

aside.title: Could an agent add the timer instead?
aside.body: Yes, and many monitoring tools do. Java agents and instrumentation pictured an agent as the stage manager who slips a note into the prompt book before rehearsal: it rewrites a method's bytecode as the class loads. Because the code itself changes, self-calls, final classes and private methods are all covered. The price is a flag on the command line, `-javaagent`, or a warning since JDK 21 when an agent attaches to a program that is already running. A container usually prefers proxies, because they need nothing from whoever starts the program.

sections.h: Retry the smallest call that is safe to repeat
sections.body:
A retry interceptor makes three promises. It only retries the failures the annotation lists: a `BookingUnavailableException` is worth another try, a seat that doesn't exist is not. It counts attempts in total, so `attempts = 3` means at most three calls. And when it gives up, the caller gets the original exception, not an `UndeclaredThrowableException` or an `InvocationTargetException` wrapped around it.

The hard part is choosing which call to repeat. Selling a ticket takes two calls to the booking service: `reserve` holds the seat, and `confirm` turns the hold into a ticket. `reserveAndConfirm` is a default method that makes both:

```java
default String reserveAndConfirm(String seat, long priceCents) {
    return confirm(reserve(seat, priceCents));
}
```

```kotlin
fun reserveAndConfirm(seat: String, priceCents: Long): String = confirm(reserve(seat, priceCents))
```

Say the first `confirm` times out. A handler that forwards the default method to the target, and retries it as a whole, repeats the reservation too. The demo's booking service keeps a list of every call it saw:

```text
container's proxy:  ticket-hold-C12, booking service saw [reserve, confirm (timed out), confirm]
  timed calls: [BookingClient.reserve, BookingClient.confirm]
retry the shell:    ticket-hold-C12, booking service saw [reserve, confirm (timed out), reserve, confirm]
```

Both halves print a ticket, and the second also held a second seat: one customer, two seats, and an empty one on the night that nobody else can buy. Through the container, `invokeDefault` runs the default body on the proxy, so each inner call carries its own `@Retry`, and the confirmation is retried as a confirmation. That's the rule for default methods from Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and the lab tests it.

Even a single call is only safe to repeat if the other side can spot the repeat. A timeout doesn't tell you the booking service didn't confirm. It tells you that you don't know. So retry `confirm` only if it carries a booking reference, the same one on every attempt, which the service uses to recognize a repeat and do the work once. The general name for such a reference is an idempotency key. The interceptor can't know whether a call carries one; the person who writes `@Retry` on the method has to.

Retries also multiply when they nest. With a subclass proxy, a retried `close` that calls a retried `verify` runs `verify`'s body up to 3 x 3 = 9 times, as the warm-up asked.

**A retry repeats whatever you annotate, harmful or not. Put `@Retry` on the smallest call that is safe to repeat, and only once along a chain of calls.**

Here the stand-in picture breaks. A real stand-in would notice the same customer coming back twice for the same seat. An interceptor notices nothing. It does exactly what the annotation says, as many times as it says.

try.title: Retry the confirmation, not the reservation
steps: Read `RetryDemo` (or the Kotlin twin). The booking service's first confirmation times out. The first half uses the container's proxy; the second uses a handler that retries every method as a whole.
Predict the list of calls the booking service sees in each half.

code.title: RetryDemo.java

alt.title: RetryDemo.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.container.l02.demo

import workbench.container.l02.Container
import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingClient
import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyBooking
import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingScript
import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.BookingUnavailableException
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler
import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException
import java.lang.reflect.Method
import java.lang.reflect.Proxy

// reserveAndConfirm, with one confirmation timing out: what does the booking service see?
fun main() {
    val c = Container(listOf(BookingScript::class.java, FlakyBooking::class.java))
    val script = c.get(BookingScript::class.java)
    script.confirmFailures.set(1)
    val result = c.get(BookingClient::class.java).reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000)
    println("container's proxy:  $result, booking service saw ${script.seen}")
    println("  timed calls: ${c.callLog().names()}")

    val naiveScript = BookingScript().apply { confirmFailures.set(1) }
    val target = FlakyBooking(naiveScript)
    val retryEverything = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> callWithRetry(target, method, a) }   // any method, defaults too
    val naive = Proxy.newProxyInstance(BookingClient::class.java.classLoader,
        arrayOf(BookingClient::class.java), retryEverything) as BookingClient
    println("retry the shell:    ${naive.reserveAndConfirm("C12", 12_000)}, booking service saw ${naiveScript.seen}")
}

private fun callWithRetry(target: Any, method: Method, a: Array<Any?>?, attempt: Int = 1): Any? =
    try {
        method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray()))                       // the default body runs on the target
    } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) {
        if (attempt == 3 || e.cause !is BookingUnavailableException) throw e.cause!!
        callWithRetry(target, method, a, attempt + 1)
    }

try.expect: Both halves return `ticket-hold-C12`. Through the container the booking service sees `[reserve, confirm (timed out), confirm]`, and the timed calls are `reserve` and `confirm`: the default method itself is not timed. The naive handler gives `[reserve, confirm (timed out), reserve, confirm]`: one customer, two seats held.

compare.title: A part a subclass can intercept, in Java and in Kotlin

java.title: ShowCloser.java

kotlin.title: ShowCloser.kt

compare.note: The two classes compile to the same shape only after you add `open` in Kotlin. Java's default is overridable, so `final` is the exception you write; Kotlin's default is final, so `open` is. That single difference decides whether a subclass proxy can work, and on an open class with a plain `fun` it fails silently. The all-open plugin flips Kotlin's default for classes with an annotation you choose. Nothing differs for JDK proxies: both languages compile interfaces to ordinary JVM interfaces, and Kotlin interface functions with a body become JVM default methods that `invokeDefault` can run.

steps.say: The theatre wants every cancellation written down with its arguments, so that a customer's complaint can be checked later. Start with the marker. It needs `RUNTIME` retention and targets methods, like `@Timed`.
Write the interceptor. It writes the call down before it passes it on, so an attempt that throws is on the record too. It doesn't catch anything: failures are the retry's business, or the caller's.

Decide where it goes in the chain. Outside `@Retry`, it writes one entry per cancellation the customer asked for. Inside, it writes every attempt. The theatre asked for every request sent to the booking service, so it goes inside: after the timer and the retry.

Teach the container that `@Recorded` counts as intercepted, in `isIntercepted`, so `check` refuses a final recorded method too. Then test through the container: a cancellation that times out once leaves two entries with the same booking reference. If it leaves one, the interceptor sits outside the retry; if it leaves none, the method was never overridden.

lab.title: Write the retry, the proxy handler and the start-up check
steps: Run the tests once. Eleven of twelve fail. The Java files in `src/main/java/.../l02` are lesson 1's solution; `Container` now hands every component to `Interception`. The Kotlin files are yours. The fixtures are in `src/test/kotlin/.../l02/Fixtures.kt`: a scripted fake booking service and a few classes the container must refuse.
Write `RetryInterceptor.intercept`: a loop around `inv.proceed()` that rethrows on the last attempt, or on an exception that isn't an instance of anything in `retryOn`.
Write `InterceptingHandler.invoke` with the four cases from its KDoc, in order. `args` is null for methods without parameters.
Write the class half of `Interception.check`: refuse a final class that has intercepted methods, then an intercepted method that is private or final, with the messages from the comment.

Run the tests. Most now fail with your own message: `ShowCloser is final, so no subclass can intercept it...`. Open `ShowCloser` and its two `@Timed` methods. Leave `hall()` final. Run until all twelve pass.
hints: In Kotlin, `Any::class.java` is `java.lang.Object`. That is what `method.declaringClass` is for `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`.
`InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *a)` needs a non-null array: use `args ?: emptyArray()` once at the top.
If `gives up after the last attempt` sees `UndeclaredThrowableException`, your target call threw the `InvocationTargetException` itself. Throw `e.cause!!`.
If the self-call test logs only `close`, `verify` is still final: `open` on the class doesn't open its members.
lab.done_when: All twelve tests in `InterceptionTest` pass, and `hall()` is still final.

drill.title: The four-case handler from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write an `InvocationHandler` for a target and a `Map<Method, List<Interceptor>>` that answers `Object` methods by identity, runs default methods with `invokeDefault`, runs every other method through its chain, and unwraps `InvocationTargetException`. Then compare. Which case did you write last, and does the order matter?

recap: An interceptor runs around a call and calls `proceed()` to pass it on; a chain of them ends in the real method. A retry calls `proceed()` again. `@Timed` outside `@Retry` times what the customer waited for.

A part with interfaces gets a JDK proxy around a separate target. The handler answers `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` by identity, runs default methods with `invokeDefault`, runs the chain, and unwraps `InvocationTargetException`.
A JDK proxy is not an instance of the class and sees only the interface's methods: ask for the interface, and put the annotations there.

A part without interfaces gets a Byte Buddy subclass, built with its real constructor arguments. It is the object itself, so self-calls are intercepted, but it can't extend a final class or override a final or private method. Kotlin is final by default: open the class and the methods, use all-open, or add an interface.
Retry only listed failures, rethrow the original, retry the inner calls of a default method one by one, and repeat only calls that carry a booking reference. Nested retries multiply.
Where today's container stops: every stand-in is made while the program starts, by reflection and by Byte Buddy, and nobody has counted what that costs. Lesson 3 measures it.
closing:
We started with a booking service that sometimes doesn't answer, and plumbing copied into every method. Now two interceptors hold the plumbing, and the container hands out stand-ins: a JDK proxy for a part with an interface, a costume copy from Byte Buddy for one without. At start-up, it refuses any annotation no proxy could reach.

Now look in your own code for a method with an annotation such as `@Transactional`, `@Retry` or `@Cacheable`. Check two things: can a proxy reach it (is it open and public?), and is it ever called through `this`?

Next, we'll measure what these stand-ins cost. How many classes does one start load, and how much of that work could the build do instead?

quiz.q: A handler has no `isDefault` branch, so the default method `reserveAndConfirm` goes through an empty chain to `method.invoke(target, args)`. `confirm` is `@Retry(attempts = 3)` on the interface, and its first call times out. What happens?
options: One reservation, two confirmations: the retry still works
One reservation and one confirmation, then the timeout reaches the caller
Two reservations and two confirmations
`invokeDefault` throws `IllegalArgumentException`
quiz.why: Forwarded to the target, the default body runs with `this` being the target, so its call to `confirm` is an ordinary call that never reaches the handler. No interceptor sees it, nothing retries it, and the timeout goes straight out. The first option is what you'd expect if annotations worked by themselves; only `invokeDefault` makes the inner calls pass through the proxy.

quiz.q: Kotlin, no compiler plugins: `open class Ushers { @Timed fun assign(seat: String) { ... } }`. A container without a start-up check builds a Byte Buddy subclass of it. What happens when a caller runs `assign("C12")`?
options: Byte Buddy throws `Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types`
The call is timed, because the subclass overrides every method
`assign` runs normally and is never timed, with no error anywhere
The JVM throws `VerifyError` when the subclass loads
quiz.why: The class is open, so subclassing works, and the first option doesn't happen. `assign` has no `open`, so kotlinc made it final, and Byte Buddy can't override a final method; it leaves it alone. The subclass inherits the original `assign`, which runs untimed. That silent case is why the lab's container checks intercepted methods for `final` when it starts.

quiz.q: You want to build this container into a GraalVM native image, a program compiled ahead of time into one machine-code file. Which part is the real obstacle?
options: The JDK proxies: native image can't run `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` at all
The singleton cells, because native image has no `volatile`
Nothing: native image supports any code that runs on HotSpot
The Byte Buddy subclasses: they are classes defined from bytes at run time, which a closed world can't contain
quiz.why: Native image builds a closed world, so every class must exist when the image is built. JDK proxies work if the reachability metadata lists each proxy's interfaces in order, so the first option is wrong. Classes that Byte Buddy writes while the program runs have no place in that world. That's one reason Quarkus generates its intercepted subclasses while the application is built.

quiz.q: Every Byte Buddy subclass in the lab is defined by its own `ByteArrayClassLoader`. After a test drops its last reference to the container, what keeps one of those loaders alive?
options: Nothing it created: the loader can be collected with its class once no instance and no reference to the class is reachable
The application class loader, which holds every child loader forever
The JIT's code cache, which pins every class it compiled
Metaspace, which is never collected
quiz.why: A class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so the chain is: container, cell, part, subclass, loader. Remove the root and the whole chain is unreachable, and a full GC can unload the class and free its metaspace. A class loader leak is the same chain with something long-lived, such as a static map or a thread local, still holding one link.

quiz.q: A part is intercepted by a subclass. `close` is `@Timed` and calls `this.verify()`, which is also `@Timed`. In what order does the lab's `CallLog` record them?
options: `close`, then `verify`
`verify`, then `close`
Only `close`, because self-calls skip the proxy
Only `verify`
quiz.why: The subclass is the object, so `this.verify()` runs `verify`'s override and its timer. Each timer records in its `finally`, when its call ends, and `verify` ends first, inside `close`. With a JDK proxy over a separate target, only `close` would be recorded, which is the third option's model.

flashcards.front: What does `proceed()` do in an interceptor chain?
flashcards.back: It runs the next interceptor, or after the last one, the real method. A retry interceptor calls it again after a listed failure.

flashcards.front: Why put `@Timed` outside `@Retry` in the chain?
flashcards.back: Then it records one call that includes every attempt: the time the caller really waited. Inside, it records each attempt separately.

flashcards.front: The four cases of a decorating `InvocationHandler`, in order?
flashcards.back: `Object` methods by identity; default methods with `invokeDefault`; the chain ending in `method.invoke(target, args)`; unwrap `InvocationTargetException`.

flashcards.front: Why can't a container return a JDK proxy for `get(FakeBooking.class)`?
flashcards.back: The proxy class extends `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` and implements only the interfaces, so it is not a `FakeBooking`. Ask for the interface.

flashcards.front: Kotlin `open class S { @Timed fun close() }`: does a Byte Buddy subclass time `close`?
flashcards.back: No, silently. `close` is final because it isn't `open`, so the subclass can't override it.

flashcards.front: Three ways to make a Kotlin class interceptable by a subclass proxy?
flashcards.back: Write `open` on the class and the intercepted methods; use the all-open plugin (or kotlin-spring); or give it an interface and use a JDK proxy.

flashcards.front: When is it safe for an interceptor to retry a booking call?
flashcards.back: When the failure is listed as worth retrying and the call carries a booking reference (an idempotency key), the same on every attempt, so the service can spot a repeat.

terms.plain: Code written once that runs around many method calls, such as a timer or a retry.
The interceptors for one method, in order; each calls proceed() to hand on to the next, and the last hands on to the method.
The real object behind a forwarding proxy, which the handler calls when the chain ends.
A generated subclass that overrides the intercepted methods and is itself the object, so self-calls are intercepted.
A Kotlin compiler plugin that makes classes with chosen annotations, and their members, open instead of final.
An ID sent with a request, such as a booking reference, so the receiver can recognize a repeat and not do the work twice.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why the container uses two kinds of proxy instead of always generating a subclass with Byte Buddy. Explain what each kind gives up, and how the container decides.
explain_back.answer: A JDK proxy needs only an interface. It works on final Kotlin classes and needs no bytecode library, but it's a separate object in front of the target: the part isn't an instance of the class, the annotations must be on the interface, and self-calls inside the target skip the interceptors. A subclass is the object itself, so self-calls are intercepted and the object is an instance of the class, but it can only intercept what it can override: no final classes, no final or private methods, which in Kotlin means writing open or using all-open. The container uses the JDK proxy whenever the component implements an interface, because that path has fewer ways to fail silently, and a subclass only when there is no interface. In both cases it checks at start-up and refuses what it can't intercept.

deeper.body:
Jakarta Interceptors, the standard behind CDI and Quarkus, has the same pieces under other names. An interceptor binding is an annotation like `@Timed` that is itself annotated `@InterceptorBinding`. The interceptor is a class with an `@AroundInvoke` method that takes an `InvocationContext` and calls `ctx.proceed()`. The order of the chain comes from `@Priority` on each interceptor class, with lower numbers running first. Spring AOP's equivalent is an AOP Alliance `MethodInterceptor`, whose `invoke(MethodInvocation)` also ends in `proceed()`, ordered by `@Order` or the `Ordered` interface.

Annotations and proxies have a quieter interaction too. Java annotations are not inherited from interfaces: `@Timed` on `BookingClient.reserve` is not visible through `FakeBooking.class.getMethod("reserve", ...)`. A JDK proxy hands the handler the interface's `Method`, so the lab's container sees it. A subclass proxy looks at the class's methods, so an annotation that lives only on an interface method would not be found there. Spring papers over this with its own annotation search, which walks interfaces and superclasses. The lab refuses the doubtful case instead: annotations on the class of an interface-proxied component are an error.

Byte Buddy can also load a generated class without a new class loader. `ClassLoadingStrategy.UsingLookup`, with a `MethodHandles.Lookup` from the part's package, defines the subclass in the same loader and package as its superclass. That lets it override package-private methods and avoids one loader per class. The lab uses the default, the simplest strategy, and lesson 3's histogram shows what it leaves behind.
